text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

SOCIAL MEDIA REGULATION IN NIGERIA

FG Shuts Down Over 13 million Social Media Accounts for Offensive Content…takes down 58.9million obscene contents

The federal government has closed down about 13,597,057 social media accounts for offensive content and violations of the code of practice by users of social media platforms such as TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, and X, formerly known as Twitter.

The government action was contained in a Code of Practice 2024 Compliance Report submitted to the government by promoters of interactive computer service platforms such as Google, Microsoft and TikTok, among others.

The Code of Practice was issued jointly by the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), and the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC).

In a statement signed on Wednesday by the Director of Corporate Communications and Media Relations of NITDA, Hajiya Hadiza Umar, the government said a total of 58,909,112 offensive contents were taken down from various platforms.

The statement, which commended Google, Microsoft, and TikTok for their continued compliance with the Code of Practice for Interactive Computer Service Platforms/Internet Intermediaries, also noted that 754,629 were “registered complaints.”
She added that 420,439 contents were removed and re-uploaded following appeals by users.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

AI-generated misinformation is becoming harder to detect. Manipulated videos, cloned voices and fabricated images can make fictional events look completely real.

The damage goes far beyond misinformation. Deepfakes can be weaponised to harass people, create non-consensual sexual content, spread rumours and sabotage personal or professional lives.

No one is immune. A person's photographs, videos or publicly available voice recordings may be misused without their knowledge or consent.

Pause before you trust what you see online. Look for the original source, check whether credible news organisations have verified the claim, and watch out for suspicious inconsistencies.

Don't turn someone else's suffering into viral content. Sharing a fake video, intimate image or unverified accusation can amplify the harm, even when you did not create it.

Act when you encounter abuse. Save relevant screenshots, links and other evidence, report the material to the platform, and seek help from the appropriate authorities.

This is a very long post about the news of the day, publicly made by an attorney on another site who frequently creates updates on H's very compete legal disputes.
It is a very important read and contains many details I had not heard until I read this, it also contains many fresh perspectives.

========
Someone makes an accusation of sexual abuse, and their story sounds very credible—because who wouldn’t believe something like that?  Only a monster, right? After all, no one would make such an accusation  if it weren’t true. That is what a great many people believe—that such  an accusation would not be made if it were not true.

But I have come across the fact that when something is presented in such a way that any criticism against it is viewed as "monstrous,"  that is precisely when it should be questioned the most.

And when I say "question," I mean that cases like these are precisely the ones that require the most investigation.

Let’s start with something some of us have had to do: moving.

Thomas Markle was living in Rosarito, Mexico. In early May 2025, he  officially moved to the Philippines. Together with his son, Thomas Jr., he settled into an apartment in Cebu City, seeking a more affordable  cost of living and medical care following the health issues he was  already dealing with.

In early 2025, weary of media harassment and seeking a lower cost  of living, Thomas decided to permanently leave his home in Mexico and  move to the Philippines. Before the trip, he began getting rid of his  belongings and packing what remained into four cardboard boxes, which  ended up being stored abroad.

That is the story Thomas Jr. is telling. But the way those boxes  were moved—and who had access to them—is not only unclear; it is also at  the heart of the ongoing legal dispute between the Markle siblings.

Let’s be clear about one thing: Thomas Sr. didn’t send those  boxes, Thomas Jr. did. He took care of it; Thomas Sr. was too ill to do  so. Didn’t Thomas Jr. check those boxes? It only makes sense to do  so—just look at the shipping cost! Imagine spending all that money, only  to discover that your father had filled them with candy wrappers.

Now, regarding such a shipment—did no one check the contents of a  box as soon as it arrived in the Philippines? I once shipped a box from  Spain to Santiago via FedEx... it was incredibly expensive! I had to  seal it in the presence of a FedEx representative, and then open it in  the presence of a representative from Correos Chile. I had to verify  that everything had arrived in good condition and that there were no  grounds for a complaint. If Thomas Sr. wanted to transport those  boxes—at such a huge financial cost—from Mexico to the Philippines, is  it really the case that no one opened them for over a year?

Now, has anyone considered a crucial detail in all of this? It was  Thomas Jr. who sent the material. So yes, he does run the risk of going  to prison. Under the strict legal framework governing international  cybercrimes, an individual who transmits child sexual abuse material  across borders can indeed face serious criminal charges, regardless of  who originally owned the material.

So, it’s not enough to just say, "Oops! Look, some material turned  up." The issue here is that Thomas Jr. sent those boxes; he was the one  with access to them; and he is the one who supposedly discovered  something inside them—in a storage unit registered in his own name.  Therefore, the question arises: didn’t Thomas Jr. check those boxes  before sending them to the Philippines?

If he cannot provide a very good explanation, he is in serious  trouble. This makes the photograph of Thomas Jr. reporting his  father—which has surfaced—highly significant. That also seems strange.  Who goes to the trouble of taking photos while reporting a crime like  this? Someone trying to create an alibi, perhaps, or looking to absolve  themselves of something?

A forensic analysis of file creation and modification dates will  be the sole factor in determining whether Thomas Jr. remains in the role  of an exemplary citizen or becomes an accused party.

Now, here’s the thing: one of the issues with Thomas Jr. is his  claim that he opened those boxes because he was looking for a phone.  Consider this: he reportedly stated that he knew there were old mobile  phones among his father’s belongings, as Thomas Sr. was a known hoarder  of technology and electronic gadgets—a habit stemming from his time  working as a television lighting director. He claims that he opened the  boxes for the sole purpose of looking for a used mobile phone to give to  the father of his Filipina girlfriend, who needed a device.

Interestingly, Thomas Markle Sr. officially retired from Hollywood in 2011

I don’t doubt that a phone from 2011 would still turn on—my Nokia  3310 does. But would it actually work? I had to give up my own Nokia in  2018 because, here in Chile, changes were made to the native GSM/2G  network infrastructure, and my SIM card stopped working. It seems Thomas  Markle had even older phones... but would they still be functional?  Philippines isn’t a developed country, but honestly—isn’t it just being  incredibly cheap to gift someone a phone from 2008, or even 2000?

Then, I ran into this issue myself: the battery. Lithium-ion  batteries from phones dating back to 2011—if left abandoned in boxes for  years—undergo a process of extreme chemical degradation. In the vast  majority of cases, they swell, become sulfated, or lose their ability to  hold a charge entirely, making it impossible to turn on the device  without keeping it permanently plugged into a power source or replacing  the battery with a new one. I’m currently frantically searching for a  battery for my 2013 Galaxy Note 3 which is the one I inherited in 2021  and use as a media player.

When a mobile phone (such as the aforementioned LG) spends years  stored in a cardboard box in a warehouse in the Philippines—a country  with extreme humidity and tropical heat—its battery undergoes an  accelerated degradation process.

Thomas Jr. alleges that the explicit video appeared on the screen  as soon as the device was turned on. In 2011, screens did not feature  intelligent auto-play systems upon startup; to view a file, a user had  to manually navigate through internal folders or MicroSD cards. And  that’s assuming the video app keeps working. Apps often stop working  because they are outdated.

Well, Thomas Jr. knew that those boxes contained old cell  phones... so, he knew that, yet he didn't check them before packing them  up? I did a thorough check of the old cell phones at my place—turning  each one on—and sent the ones that didn't work off to be recycled. But  Thomas Jr. claims he knew nothing about what was in those boxes, even  though he also says he knew they contained an old cell phone... So, did  he know or didn't he?

And as for the letter that MM allegedly received... it’s absurd. It’s complete nonsense.

The London Metropolitan Police has no legal power or authority to  investigate crimes committed in Rosarito (Mexico) by a U.S. citizen. If  anyone had wanted to report Thomas Markle in 2018, the Met would have  been the worst place in the world to do so, as they would have had to  immediately refer the report to the FBI or the Mexican police (FGR).

MM states that the letter reached the Royalty and Specialist  Protection (RaSP) unit. This unit of the Met does not investigate  ordinary or international sexual offenses; its sole function is the  physical protection of—and the assessment of security threats (such as  stalkers or terrorists) against—members of the Royal Family.

If the Met received that letter in 2018, it did not conduct a  criminal "investigation" in Mexico. The only action the RaSP could have  taken was to classify the letter as a "reputational or security risk" to  the new duchess (who had just married in May 2018) and—in a completely  irregular manner (which is why they are currently under internal  investigation)—show the letter to Meghan to warn her about the impending  scandal.

Let this be absolutely clear: an investigation was underway, yet  no charges had been filed. According to MM, a letter regarding Thomas  Markle—concerning an alleged investigation—was sent to the Met. If MM’s  account is accurate, then by handing over a file or letter containing  serious accusations made by a foreign national to a third party—in a  country other than the one where the person under investigation  resides—the police committed a grave violation of UK privacy laws,  regardless of the fact that the recipient was the individual’s daughter.  This exposes the Metropolitan Police to heavy financial penalties from  the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) and provides a legal basis  for Thomas Markle Sr. or his lawyers to file a civil lawsuit against the  Met for moral damages, defamation, and the unlawful disclosure of  confidential information.

The most significant institutional consequence is the damage to  Scotland Yard’s public reputation. The British public and legal analysts  are sharply questioning why the Royal Protection Command acted as a  private public-relations filter for the Sussexes—concealing a report of a  serious crime and handing it over to the family, rather than  transparently referring the matter to the appropriate international  agencies (such as the FBI).

There are some truly vile people in this world. If you follow the  news from Chile, you’ll know there is a massive controversy regarding  the reduction of sentences for individuals convicted of sexual offenses  against minors. Since March, 56 such convicts—without any formal  judicial review—have managed to secure this benefit, sparking criticism  from both the opposition and the ruling coalition. I am currently  feeling a level of rage and disgust that you cannot even imagine,  because these convicted individuals filed legal petitions for the  protection of constitutional rights to obtain this benefit. Disgust and  rage—I don’t even want to read the news story; I simply cannot bear it,  for reasons that go beyond the scope of this space.

However, this accusation against Thomas Markle Sr. is very  strange. Even a superficial analysis reveals that the story as we  currently know it doesn’t really hold up. Based on my own personal  experience, what Thomas Jr. has claimed just doesn’t add up. To me, it  makes no sense—because I know what it’s like to send items from one  country to another, and I also know what it’s like to own a mobile phone  from the 2000s.

And if the story of Thomas Jr. already made no sense, the  situation with MM is simply absurd—absurd from start to finish. The  narrative regarding the family rift from 2018 has been retroactively  altered to align with the current scandal of 2026. And that, I believe,  is the key detail. Why has MM done this? What is she aiming to achieve?

Meghan Markle disclosed information regarding the Metropolitan  Police because, in her hierarchy of priorities, clearing her reputation  in the face of an accusation as monstrous as abandoning her sick father  was infinitely more urgent than upholding Scotland Yard’s internal  protocols. Much like in 2021—when she failed to anticipate that the head  of the Church of England would publicly refute her claims to safeguard  the integrity of his institution—she once again assumed that London’s  Metropolitan Police would remain silent so as not to fuel the scandal.

This is really ugly.

SUBJECT: Crypto as a watch note, not a signal
ACCOUNT: @tismtruths

A crypto note in this series is a watch note. It records what was observed and the unit that observation used. It does not tell anyone what to do next. Newcomers sometimes want the note to become advice. Experienced users sometimes want it to confirm a move they already decided. Neither fits the format.

The observation can be simple: a price level was watched, a volume change was logged, a support line was noted. The unit must be written—percent, currency, or none—so no one later mixes a percentage move with a cash balance. The risk line stays at the end because crypto can go to zero. That sentence is part of the fact, not a footer.

Old chats in the archive often mixed these elements. A prompt that said “confirm the trade” or treated a gambling screen as a portfolio is labeled archive. It is useful for seeing what not to repeat. It is not a live instruction. When you turn an old log into a new note, keep the date, keep the unit, and drop any verb that directs a stranger.

The short JSON still fits in a reply so both new and old readers can check it on a phone. Ask a chat for the number, the subject, and the one fact. A pass names those three. A fail invents a wallet or a target. The note itself never places an order. It only records that something was watched.

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow.

🚨MASSIVE: India to Bring a New Satellite Internet Security Layer Through Hardware Monitoring to Track Starlink

India is preparing to add a new layer of security to satellite internet services, with a proposed hardware-based monitoring system that could give authorities greater visibility and control over satellite internet traffic operating within the country.

The move is particularly significant for Starlink, whose satellite network relies heavily on low-Earth-orbit satellites and inter-satellite links to move data across its constellation.

The proposed hardware monitor is intended to become a physical security checkpoint between satellite-internet users and foreign satellite operators. It could potentially be deployed at subscriber equipment or at satellite ground stations, creating an enforceable point through which India's security requirements can be implemented.

The system could help enforce domestic traffic routing, lawful interception, geographic restrictions, geofencing and emergency security directions. In sensitive or prohibited areas, authorities could potentially restrict satellite connectivity. 

The underlying concern is simple: India does not want critical communications infrastructure operating over its territory while remaining beyond effective Indian control.

India is therefore moving toward a model in which foreign satellite operators can enter the Indian market, but only after accepting Indian security and sovereignty requirements.

The framework is expected to apply broadly to satellite communications providers, including Starlink and other global operators. However, given Starlink's scale and technological architecture, it naturally becomes the most prominent company affected by the proposed system.

**As of mid-to-late October 2026, Starlink does not offer service in a specific set of countries and territories (per its own availability map data), while many others still lack full access due to pending launches or regulatory approval.**

### Explicitly unavailable (Starlink does not offer service; no expected date)
Starlink’s map marks these as unavailable (Roam plans generally do not work there either):

- Afghanistan  
- Belarus  
- China (including Hong Kong and Macao)  
- North Korea  
- Russia  
- Syria  

These are consistently listed as hard “not available” or blacklisted in sources that parse Starlink’s public availability data. Reasons typically involve government restrictions, licensing refusals, geopolitical issues, or national security rules (e.g., Russia has tightened rules on foreign satellite terminals).

### Awaiting regulatory approval (not commercially available yet)
Starlink lists these as waiting for national regulatory approval (no firm launch date):

- Brunei  
- India  
- Pakistan  
- Saudi Arabia  
- Thailand  
- Türkiye (Turkey)  

**Note on India**: It has received key licences (including GMPCS and IN-SPACe authorisation) and built infrastructure (e.g., gateways), but as of mid-October 2026 it still awaits final security clearances, spectrum, and related approvals. Commercial service is not available.

### Coming soon / not yet launched (many more countries)
Dozens of countries and territories are marked “coming soon,” “starting in 2026,” or “service date unknown.” Examples include various African countries (e.g., Angola, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Namibia, Tanzania, Tunisia, South Africa), some Caribbean islands, parts of Central Asia (e.g., Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan), Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Cuba, Iran, and others. Statuses can change quickly as approvals and launches proceed.

**Special cases**: Ukraine, Cyprus, and Georgia sometimes appear uncolored on maps due to border/dispute issues, but service (including Mini kits) has been available in places like Ukraine and Cyprus—check a specific address. Iran is often in the “coming soon/unknown” or effectively restricted category due to sanctions and policy.

### Key points
- Availability is country-level on the map but address-specific for ordering (capacity can limit Residential plans even where the country is live).  
- Starlink covers roughly 170+ countries/territories as available (exact counts vary slightly by source and date), with rapid expansion ongoing.  
- Statuses update frequently. For the definitive current answer, check the official map and enter an address at **[https://t.co/WFfBCRd8F1](https://t.co/YNEKcotxAn)**.

This is based on Starlink’s public map data (via aggregators) as of September–October 2026. Always verify on the official site for the latest.

INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

The Off Switch

At six in the evening on 13 January 2026, ahead of Uganda's general election, the Uganda Communications Commission announced an internet shutdown. Amnesty International reported that the regulator said it would "remain in effect until further notice."

For a founder, "until further notice" is the hardest phrase in the language to plan around. You cannot tell customers when you will be back, or staff whether to come in. Payments, orders, support messages and the cloud tools your company runs on all sit on the far side of a switch someone else controls.

The shutdown lasted 101 hours, according to a Top10VPN estimate reported by Context, the Thomson Reuters Foundation's news service, which put the cost at $3.8 million a day and about $16 million in total. When the government lifted the nationwide block, it said it would keep social media platforms blocked, The Hindu reported on 18 January.

We had been here before. Uganda switched the internet off for about five days around its January 2021 election, starting on 13 January, an outage confirmed by four independent network datasets. The Internet Society's COST tool estimated it cost the economy around US$9 million. The Facebook block imposed that year was still in place in early 2025, according to Access Now.

A five-day shutdown is an outage. A platform block that runs for four years changes which channels a small business can build on, and every Ugandan founder who planned a launch around social media since 2021 has had to plan around that too.

Switch risk

Every other line of the constraint tax leaves a founder something to do. When the power goes, you start a generator. When the road closes, you take a side road. When data is expensive, you ration it. A government shutdown offers nothing to buy and no way around. I call this switch risk: the chance that the whole network your business runs on is turned off by a decision you hear about after it is made, with an end date you also learn late. In 2021 and again in 2026 it arrived in the same week as the vote, so I now treat the election calendar as part of every plan.

Switch risk is priced by people who never see it happen. A client abroad who lost four days of contact in January weighs that the next time a contract comes up. An investor running diligence asks about the hole in your January metrics. The founder did nothing to lose that trust and pays for it anyway.

The cost lands hardest outside the telcos. CEO East Africa Magazine (@CEOEastAfrica) studied Airtel and MTN Uganda's figures and estimated that the four-day shutdown "may have wiped out as much as UGX 24 billion in data revenues." Michael Niyitegeka (@niyimic), executive director of Refactory in Kampala and country manager for ICDL Africa in Uganda, answered on X the next day: "Focusing on the telcos IMO is missing the wider implications of this on the digital enabled or dependent services or businesses."

I agree with him. The telcos' losses appear in a quarterly report. The delivery startup that lost four days of orders, the freelancer who missed a deadline for a client in Europe, the training program that went silent in the middle of a cohort: those losses are recorded nowhere.

People improvised. People Daily (@PeopleDailyKe) reported that Bitchat, an offline messaging app, had become "a key lifeline for Ugandans cut off from the internet." The other workarounds I hear about are slow ones: queuing work for the day the connection returns, phoning customers one by one, carrying documents across town.

Who reaches for the switch

The comparison with rich democracies is stark, and it holds up like for like, because one organization counts every country with the same definition in the same year. Access Now and the KeepItOn coalition documented at least 313 internet shutdowns in 52 countries in 2025, a new record. Their 2025 report logs none for the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Estonia, Australia or New Zealand. The only United States entry is a single platform, TikTok, which went dark for 14 hours after the Supreme Court upheld a ban on national security grounds, before service was restored.

Democracy alone does not protect a network. India, often held up as a model digital economy, imposed 84 shutdowns in 2024 and 65 in 2025, according to the same coalition's reports. Kenya logged 3 in 2025. In October 2024, The Kenya Times (@thekenyatimes) reported that Safaricom's chief executive, Peter Ndegwa, had apologized to Kenyans over the internet shutdown during that year's protests. Ethiopia has run regional shutdowns since November 2020 in Tigray and since August 2023 in Amhara.

Nigeria tried a narrower version. The federal government blocked Twitter for 222 days, ending on 13 January 2022, Paradigm Initiative reported. JJ. Omojuwa (@Omojuwa), founder of BGX and Alpha Reach, marked the milestone in November 2021: "It's now been 5 full months since Twitter was blocked in Nigeria by the Nigerian government". For businesses that found their customers on the platform, that was more than seven months with the shop door locked from outside.

Latin America's founders describe a different cut. In Venezuela, shopkeepers told Venezolana de Prensa (@VENPRENSA) in May 2026 that the internet, card terminals and mobile payments all fail during electricity rationing. The shutdown counts I gathered for this series do not single out Brazil, Argentina or Mexico, so I leave them out of this comparison instead of guessing.

Some cuts happen by accident. In May 2024, subsea cable cuts off East Africa dropped internet traffic in Kenya and Uganda by 10 to 25% at first, Cloudflare's monitoring showed. And the global bill is large. Top10VPN, using the NetBlocks COST model, estimates that government-imposed shutdowns cost the world economy $19.7 billion in 2025. That figure comes from a model, so I use it for scale and keep it out of any budget.

Why the switch gets used

When Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson shared the 2024 economics prize for their work on why some countries stay poor, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences summarized their findings in one sentence: "Societies with a poor rule of law and institutions that exploit the population do not generate growth or change for the better." It also explained why such systems last: "extractive institutions provide short-term gains for the people in power."

A shutdown is a clean example. The gain, a quieter information space for a few days, goes to whoever holds power. The cost goes to everyone who sells, learns or works online, and none of them gets a say in the order. Most of them learn about it at the same moment as everyone else.

The evidence on the other side of the switch is strong. Hjort and Poulsen, writing in the American Economic Review in 2019, studied the arrival of fast internet across 12 African countries and found that it raised employment, and that "increased firm entry, productivity, and exporting contribute to higher net job creation." A connection that stays on creates firms. A connection that can be switched off teaches people to build less on it.

They were once here

The habit of giving notice before the state changes people's working lives is younger than it looks. In the United States, the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 was written in part "to provide for public participation in the rulemaking process, for instance through public commenting." Notice and comment turned a decision into a process that people could see coming.

Other countries went further and treated the network as public infrastructure. South Korea set up a four-year plan, Cyber Korea 21, in March 1999, with a broadband deployment program inside it, and in the 1990s it was in a minority of governments giving low-interest loans to telecom providers for high-speed lines, the OECD recorded. By mid-2001, Korea had 14 broadband subscribers per 100 inhabitants against an OECD average of 2. Estonia proposed its Tiger Leap program, with its emphasis on education, in 1996, and launched the first version of its X-Road system in 2001. Both countries made the network something the state itself runs on, and a state that runs on the network has every reason to keep it switched on.

The case for the switch

Governments give reasons for these orders, usually security around elections or protests, and I am poorly placed to judge every one. Some may have prevented real harm. I may also be underestimating how many businesses here route around a shutdown with VPNs, and how much work simply waits and resumes. My sense of the damage could be too high.

What I can judge is the cost to the people building here, and that cost rarely enters the room when the switch is thrown. A shutdown teaches a particular helplessness. I have watched capable founders spend those days refreshing a phone, unable to work and unable to rest. The messages stop, the news thins out, and you are left guessing whether clients abroad are still waiting.

What should change

Governments that keep the power to shut networks down should bind it by rule: a published legal basis, a stated scope and a stated end date, the kind of notice an American statute required for ordinary regulations eighty years ago. A shutdown with an end date still stops the business, yet a founder can plan around a date.

Investors and partners can stop penalizing founders for gaps the state created. A four-day hole in the January metrics of a company in an election year explains itself, and a diligence process that treats it as a warning sign is measuring the government.

Donors and development banks that fund connectivity can attach the same condition to their money that they attach to procurement: published rules for when it can be turned off.

Founders can build for the switch. Keep customer phone numbers somewhere you can reach offline. Keep a second channel, such as SMS or a phone tree, for the customers who matter most. Agree in advance with your team how you will communicate if data goes dark. Tell clients abroad, before an election, that a blackout is possible, and write it into contracts where the work is time-bound. These steps shorten the recovery. The business still stops.

If you run a company or a founder program that depends on the internet in a country where it can be switched off, I can help you build the evidence and the contingency plan well before the next election. Book a strategy call at https://t.co/ZsS6d5KfGO.

Has a shutdown ever cost your business a customer, and what did you change afterwards?

It has become fashionable these days to abuse IITs and their faculties. I get it, freedom of speech, healthy skepticism of institutions, all fair game. 

But before that fashionable takedown becomes the whole story, sit with this 1 fact for a second....

Right now, last month, IIT profs have put more free, peer-reviewed, university grade course content into the world than any other institution on the planet, and most Indians have never watched a single hour of it.

2001....

A handful of IIT directors come back from a trip to Carnegie Mellon, having seen an American prof build an entire functioning university around teaching people online. 

They are stunned enough to try replicating it for India, in engineering, at a scale nobody had attempted before.

The idea finally took shape under Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government. The man holding the HRD portfolio through that entire stretch, 1998-2004, was Murli Manohar Joshi, himself a physics prof before he was ever a minister. 

On January 26, 2003, months before NPTEL's own official rollout that year, Joshi Ji personally inaugurated a companion initiative, the Eklavya Technology Channel, explicitly built to beam actual IIT classrooms into homes across the country. 

7 IITs and the IISc quietly went live. 

No press conference most people remember. Just profs, cameras, and a govt that wrote the check for something nobody could fully prove would work.

The word "MOOC" did not even exist yet. Coursera and edX launched in 2012. 

The term was not even coined until 2008. NPTEL was already recording real lectures years before Silicon Valley invented free online university education and got magazine covers for it. 

India did not copy the MOOC revolution, it built one of the first drafts before anyone had a name for it.

Fast forward to now. 

NPTEL is the largest repository of engineering and science course content on Earth: 

- 56,000+ hours of lectures

-3,200+ courses

- a YouTube channel with 1.86B views and 5.6M subscribers

...built entirely by government-funded faculty, not a venture-backed edtech company. 

Not entertainment.... 

Thermodynamics. Signal processing. Soil mechanics. Quantum Mechanics. 

Built by profs people love to mock as "out of touch," "irrelevant," "stuck in an old system."

A student in rural Bihar with a smartphone has, right now, the same lecture an IIT KGP student sat through, free, no JEE rank required. 

And yet ask most students outside the IIT system if they have done a single NPTEL certification, and you will mostly get silence. 

Employers still do not weight it the way they weight a foreign MOOC certificate with a fraction of the rigor. The exact students this was built for often do not know it exists.

If a country builds the largest free reservoir of elite education on the planet, a decade ahead of everyone else, and barely drinks from it, is that the institution's failure / ours, for criticizing loudly and never once checking what is already free and sitting right there?

Criticize the IITs all you want, no institution should be above scrutiny. But this particular story deserves the same volume as the criticism. It just never gets it.

Article 19 of the Indian Constitution guarantees 6 fundamental freedoms to citizens, subject to reasonable restrictions.

 1⃣Speech & Expression (Art. 19(1)(a)): Encompasses press freedom and broadcasting, subject to state security, public order, and defamation.

2⃣Peaceful Assembly (Art. 19(1)(b)): Allows unarmed assembly for protests, restricted under public order and sovereignty grounds.

3⃣Form Associations (Art. 19(1)(c)): Covers unions and parties, excluding the right to strike, under public order and morality limits.

4⃣Move Freely (Art. 19(1)(d)): Grants nationwide movement, restricted for public interest or Scheduled Tribe protection.

5⃣Reside & Settle (Art. 19(1)(e)): Allows residence anywhere in India subject to similar public and tribal safeguards.

6⃣Profession & Trade (Art. 19(1)(g)): Permits carrying out any trade or profession, subject to public interest and state qualifications.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

text:
Ireland put the tweeter on trial, not the groper

I cannot believe the resources the state has mustered to go after a guy for making a tweet.

I'm writing this on the lunch break of Kirk Loco's trial in Bray, County Wicklow, about an hour south of Dublin. Kirk is being prosecuted for a tweet warning young women about migrant men harassing girls on a public bus. The tweet was true. And the man he warned about was in the courtroom today as the prosecution's main witness.

I can't identify him. He's a refugee claimant, and the lawyers and police warned me not to say anything that could reveal who he is. I'll say only that he needed an Arabic translator.

He testified he did nothing wrong, that he was just looking for a place to plug in his phone. Then he said his phone fell on the floor, which is why he got up and sat down next to the teenage girls. He never explained why he moved from the seat in front of them to the seat beside them, blocking the aisle.

According to the girl, he groped her, his belt was undone and his pants were so low his pubic hair was visible. She was so frightened she fled downstairs on the double-decker bus.

How do we know all this? There were about 10 CCTV cameras on that bus. They show him moving back and forth around the girl. They show that when the bus stopped and it was clear he was in trouble, he went to the back and played possum. Thirty-eight seconds from chatting to another passenger to out cold.

The driver testified he was obviously faking. Asked about that, he told the court: “I'm known as a very quick sleeper.”

I've been to 100 trials in my life, maybe more, and I don't think I've ever seen a shiftier witness. He took two or three positions on every question and switched mid-answer. I don't think the judge was buying it either.

Laoise de Brún, the barrister we're crowdfunding for Kirk, sliced and diced him on cross-examination. It was like shooting fish in a barrel.

Then a senior Garda took the stand and talked about the refugee accommodation at Newtownmountkennedy. He described the migrant men there as “vulnerable.”

Irish teenage girls are allegedly being harassed, and the men are the vulnerable ones?

He also described an incident where men from that centre were filming young girls at a sporting event. His response was to have them delete the videos — he deleted the evidence.

There's a term in psychology, DARVO: deny, attack, reverse victim and offender. That's what I watched today. The whole system is upside down. The hero of this story, according to the prosecution, is a man who admitted touching this girl and having his pants down. The villain is the man who warned the neighbourhood.

This is Kirk's 10th court appearance. He faces possible jail. The trial is only half over, and I'll have more from inside the courtroom.

If you want to help pay for Kirk's lawyers, and for Hugh Fagan, who goes on trial Tuesday, please go to https://t.co/SewO5oD5BL.

I don't think I'm easily shocked. I've seen too much. But I have never seen anything like this. Ireland needs help.
